own_scenes.desc: «Eve of Destruction», que definió y mató la «protesta» como género efímero, provocó una avalancha de discos de respuesta: «The Dawn of Correction» de los Spokesmen, «The Revolution Kind» de Sonny Bono, «What’s Come Over This World» de Billy Carr; y el «Universal Soldier» de Donovan, «The Universal Coward» de Jan Berry. El examen más claro de la mentalidad patriótica estaba en el country, que desde mediados de los sesenta se volvió reaccionario: un baluarte frente a los cambios y frente a una cultura juvenil incomprensible, blanco, de pueblo, de clase obrera y media baja (precisamente las clases más golpeadas por la guerra), con valores cristianos y patriotismo sin preguntas; George Wallace ya lo había usado en su campaña de 1964. «The Ballad of the Green Berets» fue su apoteosis; después llegaron «Day for Decision» de Johnny Sea y «Gallant Men» del senador Everett Dirksen.

refs.q: The loudest noise had been made by Barry McGuire’s ‘Eve of Destruction’, the record that both defined and killed ‘Protest’ as a short-lived genre.
refs.para: The loudest noise had been made by Barry McGuire’s ‘Eve of Destruction’, the record that both defined and killed ‘Protest’ as a short-lived genre. Hitting #1 at the end of September, it polarised the country. There were plenty of hooks in the song to upset the public: lines that linked Red China to Selma, Alabama; that pointed out the paradox whereby a young man could serve in the armed forces (at the age of eighteen) but could not vote (until the age of twenty-one).
refs.chapter: Marzo: The Ballad of the Green Berets: la guerra de Vietnam en Estados Unidos

refs.q: Country hadn’t always been reactionary, but from the mid-1960s onwards it became so
refs.para: The success of ‘The Ballad of the Green Berets’ was the apotheosis of this country music groundswell. It seems strange that one particular genre of music should have been so associated with the patriotic viewpoint, but there were firm reasons for the link. Country hadn’t always been reactionary, but from the mid-1960s onwards it became so: a bulwark against the rapid changes in American life and a safe haven from an increasingly incomprehensible youth culture.

similar_scenes.name: Nelly y los St. Lunatics
similar_scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
similar_scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
similar_scenes.desc: Ningún rapero de St. Louis había llegado al gran público; los St. Lunatics (Murphy Lee, Ali, Kyjuan, City Spud, Slo’ Down) tuvieron éxito regional con «Gimme What U Got» (1997) y, sin contrato de grupo, empujaron a Nelly en solitario a Universal. Country Grammar (2000), producido casi entero por Jay E en un estudio de una pista de patinaje donde no se podía fumar, fue número 1 más de un mes: sing-alongs de pop-rap con acento del Medio Oeste, el canto que heredaría Drake.

similar_scenes.name: Blues funky y blues clásico
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: Del grito de los esclavos a las fiestas de sábado por la noche en los campos de algodón, el blues rural cumplía la misma función que la música africana. Con la urbanización de la Primera Guerra Mundial llegó el primer blues grabado, el «blues clásico» de Bessie y Mamie Smith, a menudo picante («Need a Little Sugar in My Bowl»), y el hot jazz de Louis Armstrong, que asustó a los críticos y abrió el mercado de los «race records».
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: blues, jazz, gospel y R&B

similar_scenes.name: La geografía del metal: del Black Country al mundo
similar_scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
similar_scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
similar_scenes.desc: La subcultura nace en Gran Bretaña, en el norte industrial (Birmingham, las Midlands; Londres nunca fue meca del metal), hacia 1973. Unos años después se asienta en Estados Unidos, en las grandes ciudades del Medio Oeste y los suburbios obreros, no en las costas «hip»; Canadá la tiene a finales de los setenta en torno a Toronto, y Alemania desde mediados de los setenta, con efecto en las ventas en 1981. Se extiende por el norte de Europa y Escandinavia; Polonia es el primer país del bloque del Este con una subcultura seria, porque su radio estatal emitía programas de heavy, y tras la caída del Muro los jóvenes del Este compran discos de Bon Jovi, AC/DC, Metallica y Led Zeppelin. En 1989 Ozzy y otros tocan en Moscú. Japón se suma pronto y en los ochenta llega a Brasil y México, donde la cultura de la muerte resuena con el thrash y el death. Hace falta cierta prosperidad juvenil y que la cultura propia (el islam, una lucha política) no absorba a los jóvenes. La prensa metal celebra la gira de Iron Maiden por Polonia en 1984 como prueba de una comunidad internacional.
similar_scenes.family: Cultura metal: público, medios y conciertos

similar_scenes.name: Country blues
similar_scenes.author: Ted Gioia
similar_scenes.desc: La cara liberadora y dionisíaca del ritmo africano: un medio para expresar dolor, opresión y deseo sin autocompasión, con un efecto catártico comparable al de la tragedia. Lo conocemos por grabaciones a partir de los años veinte. Forma de doce compases (tónica, dominante, subdominante) con blue notes que oscilan entre tercera mayor y menor, y estrofa AAB; pero los cantantes del campo alargan o acortan los compases a su antojo porque cantan solos con su guitarra. Charlie Patton, más antiguo y ligado a la plantación, dialoga con su guitarra; Blind Lemon Jefferson canta agudo y fino en Texas; Leadbelly, descubierto en una cárcel por los Lomax, acaba en Nueva York; Robert Johnson, tardío y casi desconocido en vida, se convierte en el paradigma del Delta. Gioia duda del origen en los griots africanos: el blues es un tipo de canción nuevo, nacido en el Sur.
similar_scenes.family: Raíces: África, blues, ragtime y espirituales

similar_scenes.name: Country-rock y roots-rock
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: En los setenta, el reajuste a los viejos valores (blues, folk, country) convierte al rock en uno de los mayores éxitos del consumismo: el Establishment ya no intenta destruirlo, lo absorbe. El country-rock de Gram Parsons es una moda enorme: Commander Cody, New Riders Of The Purple Sage, Manassas, Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Poco y los Eagles (Desperado, Hotel California); en Nashville surgen los «outlaws» (Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson). El roots-rock sigue con Hot Tuna, Little Feat y Doobie Brothers, y la nostalgia recupera el blues (Roy Buchanan, Bonnie Raitt), la armonía vocal (Manhattan Transfer, Roches, McGarrigle Sisters) y los cincuenta (American Graffiti).

similar_scenes.name: Alt-country
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: La revolución iniciada en Chicago por Souled American y Uncle Tupelo (No Depression: baladas country con la furia del hardcore) se convierte en los noventa en un género propio: sus herederos abandonan el hardcore por los sonidos más espartanos y tradicionales. Son Volt de Jay Farrar y Wilco de Jeff Tweedy (Being There, Yankee Hotel Foxtrot); Will Oldham (Palace) arranca el movimiento; Freakwater, Ida, Handsome Family, Retsin, Blue Mountain, Whiskeytown, Grant Lee Buffalo, Citizens' Utilities, Willard Grant Conspiracy. El «chamber folk» de Lambchop, Lullaby For The Working Class, Geraldine Fibbers y Pinetop Seven; el country-rock de Volebeats, Ass Ponys, Sixteen Horsepower, Old 97's y los terroristas Grifters; el folk-rock de Swell, Counting Crows, Cracker, Cake, Hootie & The Blowfish; los Black Crowes; Belle And Sebastian, Arab Strap y los polacos Atman.

works.name: When I Was a Cowboy: Early American Songs of the West, Volume 2

podcast.title: Jukebox Popularity (Pre-1937)
podcast.body: Jukeboxes were significant in popularizing country music, along with R&B and rock and roll, before 1937. The devices were so widely used that their popularity was linked to a national coin shortage. "Jukeboxes helped spread the word on R&B country and rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

podcast.title: Growth During Musicians' Strike (1942)
podcast.body: During the American Federation of Musicians strike of 1942, country musicians were not considered "real musicians" by the performing rights organization ACAPE, and thus were not covered by recording prohibitions. This loophole allowed them to continue making records, leading to a rapid spread of country music in the absence of new Big Band recordings. "Acape also did not consider country musicians, western performers, and R&B acts to be real musicians. As a result, they were not covered by any prohibitions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections

podcast.title: Early Categorization (1955)
podcast.body: In 1955, "country" was one of the four main categories used to classify popular music, alongside rock, pop, and R&B. This simple classification system was prevalent before the extensive fragmentation of rock and roll. "In the beginning, and I'm talking about, about 1955, it was easy to categorize popular music. There was rock, pop, country, and R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Power Pop

podcast.title: Genre Segregation in Charts (1956)
podcast.body: Despite Fats Domino's "Blueberry Hill" being listed among Billboard's top 30 country sellers for the year, it never appeared on the top 100 country charts in 1956, illustrating strict genre segregation. This incident marked the sole appearance by a black artist on any Billboard country charts in the 1950s, highlighting a disparity between audience purchasing habits and industry gatekeepers' recognition. "Blueberry Hill made Billbud's top 30 records of the year for country sales in his annual round-up, but it never appeared even on the top 100 country charts during 1956 itself."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Presence in Million Dollar Quartet Session (1956)
podcast.body: A substantial portion of the music played during the Million Dollar Quartet jam session consisted of "pure country music," alongside Southern Gospel, indicating the genre's strong presence among these rock and roll pioneers. "But otherwise what they're playing is either pure country music or what's euphemistically called Southern Gospel."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Shift in Artist Promotion (1956)
podcast.body: By December 1956, artists like Johnny Cash began to be promoted specifically as country singers, signaling a genre differentiation that was taking place. Many artists also moved increasingly into country music after this period. "Johnny Cash had started to be promoted as a country singer, rather than a rock and roller."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Plane Crash Victim (1963)
podcast.body: Country singer Patsy Cline died on March 5, 1963, when the small Piper aircraft she was traveling in crashed in a forest near Camden, Tennessee, during bad weather. Her death was a significant loss to the country music genre. "March 5th, 1963, Country Singer Patsy Klein was a passenger in a small, piper aircraft that went down in bad weather in a forest near Camden, Tennessee."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Airplanes!

podcast.title: National Reach in 1976
podcast.body: With the premiere of "Austin City Limits" on PBS in January 1976, country music demonstrated its move from being a regional genre to having a national presence. "with this move we can see how country music is no longer regional it's national."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 31 - The Spirit of '76 - Pop Music on America's Bicentennial

podcast.title: Major Type of Popular Music (Pre-1977)
podcast.body: Prior to 1977, country was considered one of the few major types of popular music, alongside pop, rock, and R&B, under which all music could be broadly grouped. "Up until about 1977 there were only a few major types of popular music. You had pop, you had rock, you had country, and R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Snob

podcast.title: Pre-1978 Categorization
podcast.body: Country music was one of the four principal genres of popular music before 1978, each with its own flavor, allowing for easy categorization. "Before 1978, things were fairly simple...We had rock, we had pop, we had country, we had R&B."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: "White Man's Soul Music" (1991)
podcast.body: Chris Christofferson described country music in 1991 as "white man's soul music," focusing on themes of drinking, cheating, and sex as subjects not typically found in pop music. This perspective, however, is considered problematic for implicitly excluding black performers and fans. "country is white man's soul music."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Underrepresentation in Pre-SoundScan Charts (Before May 25, 1991)
podcast.body: Under the old, unreliable sales reporting system, country music was one of two genres found to be significantly underrepresented. SoundScan's accurate data revealed its true popularity. "Two genres of music were found to have been greatly underrepresented under the old system. The first was country"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Amazing Year That Was 1991

podcast.title: Yeehaw Challenge Meme (2018-2019)
podcast.body: The "Yeehaw Challenge" was a cultural meme circulating within the country music world around 2018-2019. It played a significant role in the initial viral spread and chart success of Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road." "It just so happened that there was a meme in the country music world at the time called the Yeehaw Challenge. And Montero's song got swept up in it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 3: (80-71)

podcast.title: "Good Old Boys Network" (Contemporary)
podcast.body: The contemporary country music industry, particularly in Nashville, is still characterized as a "good old boys network," which contributes to the current gender inequality where female voices are underrepresented on radio. "Reba McIntyre said that none of that surprises her because Nashville is still a good old boys network"

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 23 - Women of Country Music in the 70s

podcast.title: "The Pill" Controversy
podcast.body: The genre experienced internal conflict when Loretta Lynn's record label, reflecting conservative sentiments, initially refused to release her song "The Pill" in 1972 due to its controversial celebration of female reproductive freedom. This event highlighted the tension between traditional country values and emerging discussions on sexual liberation. "However, Loretta's record label would not release this record until 1975."

podcast.body: By the 1990s, Mut Lang was scoring on the country charts through his partnership with country megastar Shania Twain, whose "Twangi hits" carried his signature stadium-rocking qualities, demonstrating his genre versatility. "by the 90s, Mut was scoring on the country charts too, mostly through his partnership, professional and personal, with country megastar Shania Twain."

podcast.title: Nashville Industrial Complex
podcast.body: This term is used to describe the established country music industry in Nashville, which has historically rebuffed artists who record country music but are perceived as outsiders, including Black artists and those attempting to cross over to pop. "rebuffed by what I call the Nashville industrial complex."

podcast.title: Nashville's Conservatism in Recording
podcast.body: Despite being deeply rooted in the music industry, Nashville was surprisingly conservative when it came to adopting new recording technology and techniques. This was evident in the resistance to rubato and the traditional practice of recording all musicians in one room. "I've seen this story written about three different early Orbison songs, and it could have been any of them, but the descriptions of the running scared session are the most detailed."

podcast.title: Origins and Influences
podcast.body: The roots of country music are a blend of black and white influences. What was once known as Hillbilly music during the World War I era saw black and white musicians playing together and influencing each other. The banjo is an African instrument, and songs like "Will the Circle Be Unbroken" originated as African American spirituals, demonstrating the genre's diverse heritage. "The roots of country music are black and white."

podcast.title: Personal Dislike Despite Familiarity
podcast.body: Despite efforts to increase cognitive familiarity with country music, including spending time in Nashville, interacting with the country community, hanging out with hardcore fans, interviewing musicians, and attending shows, the speaker still finds they "can't stand it." This illustrates that while knowing about a genre often increases enjoyment, it doesn't always guarantee liking it. "But no matter how much I try to increase my cognitive familiarity with all aspects of country music, I just can't stand it."

podcast.title: Prevalence of Alcohol References
podcast.body: A notable characteristic of country music is its frequent mention of alcohol; statistics show that one in five country music songs contains some reference to alcohol. "One in five country music songs have some reference to alcohol."

podcast.title: RCA's Green Vinyl Coding
podcast.body: In an attempt to color-code records by genre, RCA designated green vinyl for country music releases. This system was part of the initial launch of the 7-inch single but did not last long. "Country was green."

podcast.title: Race Problem
podcast.body: Country music, similar to rock, has historically had and continues to have a "race problem" where opportunities and representation for non-white artists are limited. "There is no question that country music like rock has a race problem. I'm not saying had it still has a race problem."

podcast.title: Radio Format Alternative
podcast.body: In January 1993, a radio station considered flipping to a country music format, which was a "real possibility." However, new management ultimately decided to double down on an alternative format instead, after observing the rise of grunge and Lollapalooza. "Instead of flipping the station to country, which had been a real possibility, they looked around and saw that Grunge was happening."

podcast.body: Black artists, such as Ray Charles with his 1962 LP 'Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music,' have historically faced difficulty being accepted by the country music industry, with his album topping pop and R&B charts but not country. "Black artists in particular have had a tough time."

podcast.body: The steel guitar, an evolution of the Hawaiian lap-style guitar where a metal slide (the "steel") is used, became a significant instrument and sound in country music. podcast.title: Segregated Billboard Charts
podcast.body: The racial division in the United States extended to the music industry, where even Billboard's music charts were segregated. This segregation reinforced the perception that country music was for white audiences and other genres for black audiences. "even billboards music charts were segregated."

podcast.body: Country music "did not rate at all" on playlists specifically designed for sexual encounters. Despite this, country fans were found to be the most likely to have participated in an orgy and the least likely to use any form of protection. "country did not rate at all."

podcast.title: Shift from Traditional Sound (1970s)
podcast.body: In the 1970s, country radio actively moved away from traditional elements like fiddles and banjos, even though these are considered essential pieces of traditional country music. "The growth of country radio which began in the late 1960s and was in full effect by the 1970s has very little to do with fiddles and banjos that really are an essential piece of traditional country music."

podcast.title: Skepticism Towards Rock Singers
podcast.body: Some country singers and their fans were concerned that rock singers entering the country genre were insincere in their appreciation or were making fun of country music. The differing approaches to music-making, such as a rock artist's desire to "play what you feel" versus a country session player's preference for specific instructions, fueled this suspicion. "They were worried that the rock singers were not sincere about their appreciation for country. Their approach to making the music might have been a little different, too, which leads to questions about whether or not they were serious."

podcast.title: Slow Adoption of Streaming (2010s)
podcast.body: Country music fans were among the slowest to adopt streaming as a primary way of listening to music in the 2010s, contrasting with the rapid embrace by other genres like pop and hip hop. This indicates a resistance or slower transition for certain fan bases to new technologies. "Fans of two specific genres were very slow to adopt this new way of listening. There were country music fans and rock fans."

podcast.title: SoundScan Impact on Charts
podcast.body: The addition of SoundScan to Billboard's charts in 1991 significantly boosted the fortunes of country music on the pop charts. SoundScan's accurate tallying of music sales allowed genres that previously underperformed on pop charts to gain more accurate representation and higher positions. "Sound Scan boosted the fortunes of genres that had never done so well on the pop charts before, including country music."

podcast.title: Spread through Migration and Technology
podcast.body: In the 1920s, the industrialization-driven migration from the South to other parts of the country, coupled with the rise of radio and the recording industry, rapidly extended Country music across the United States. "Con la migración de los años 20 del sur al resto del país, impulsada por la industrialización, y en la hoje de la radio y el surgimiento de la industrial discográfica, la música a un triuces extendió rápidamente por todos los Estados Unidos."

podcast.title: Storytelling Heart
podcast.body: At its core, country music is a storyteller's genre, celebrating the ability to tell compelling narratives. This tradition stems from multicultural and multiracial origins, rooted in the traditional ballad or folk song introduced to the South by British immigrants, and incorporating rhythmic influences and instruments like the banjo from Africa, contributing to "hillbilly music." "At the heart of country music is the story. It is a story tellers genre."

podcast.body: Tom Parker, despite not personally liking music, chose to enter country music management.
